circularityGuidelines.guideline_primary: Use durable and robust components and materials.

circularityGuidelines.comment: Divide the product into different modules, and place all the parts that need to be exchanged or upgraded into one single module, thus lowering the effort needed to upgrade the product.

circularityGuidelines.comment: Avoid cross-dependences between modules; otherwise, we might be forced to update a working module simply as a consequence of updating an outdated one.

circularityGuidelines.comment: Make it possible to modernize and upgrade the product by simple replacement of modules by the end-user without damaging the product. It might also be a good means of placing parts that are supposed to be replaced in a module, such as batteries or wear parts.

circularityGuidelines.guideline_primary: Design in modular construction.
circularityGuidelines.comment: Modularity of products for reuse should be user oriented to help with adapting the product to new users. It might thus become a driving force for reuse.

circularityGuidelines.guideline_secondary: Make spare parts and exchange components easily available.
circularityGuidelines.comment: Repair and maintenance are only viable if components of products are easily found on the market and preferably provided inexpensively.

circularityGuidelines.guideline_secondary: Use joints and connectors that can be easily opened and closed multiple times.
circularityGuidelines.comment: Reversible fasteners that can be reused are good.
Mark where fasteners are located to ease dismantling.
Use inseparable joints and connectors for components made of the same material or compatible material.
minimize the number of connectors and joints.
Make it easy to disassemble the product with as few ordinary tools as possible.
Use fastening devices that can be easily opened and closed multiple times.

Latches, snaps and clips are normally preferred to screws and bolts for time efficiency reasons. Prioritize latches, snaps, clips and bolts and screws over welding, rivets, folding, staples, and gluing, all of which make a joint more difficult to demount.
Snap fasteners and latching are good for disassembly.
Screws are normally good for disassembly.
Adhesives and glues are generally not preferred if the product must be dismantled for remanufacturing.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: REPMs are embedded in the motor, requiring partial transmission disassembly before the motor and rotor can be reached.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: The number and order of preceding components are part of the recovery burden before magnet extraction is considered.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Preceding components; access layers; rotor location within transmission
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The study evaluates a Ford Fusion HF35 transmission. It does not evaluate individual magnet extraction.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The case contained 43 connectors, including 35 bolts; fastener disconnection accounted for 67% of total disassembly time.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: High connector and bolt counts were a dominant contributor to access effort in the analysed transmission.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Number of fasteners; connector count; connector type
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: Time values are case-specific and depend on the authors' disassembly model and sequence.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: A design scenario reduced transmission-cover bolts from 21 to 11.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: The modelled manual disassembly time fell from about 5.0 min to about 3.8 min, directly linking connector count to disassembly effort.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Fastener count on access-critical covers
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: This is a modelled design-for-disassembly scenario rather than a physical redesign experiment.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Motor architecture and number of access layers
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The Mazda dual-rotor same-axis design required removal of two casings and additional manipulation before both rotors could be accessed.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Additional casings, screws, precision-fit removals and repositioning increased the recorded disassembly burden.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Rotor arrangement; number of casings; preceding removals
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The authors state that Toyota and Mazda should not be treated as a controlled design comparison because power, torque and vehicle applications differ.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Toyota required 31 screws and Mazda 36; different screw forms and sizes, including thread-locking fluid, were encountered.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Different screw sizes increased tool changeovers, while some screw locations had limited tool-access clearance.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Fastener count; fastener type; size variation; locking compound; tool clearance
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: Counts apply to the two case-study motors and the selected disassembly boundary.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Top casings, stators and rotors included tight or precision fits.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: These joints required specialised removal actions rather than simple gripping or lifting.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Fit type; presence of alignment pins; removal access point
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The observed difficulty is partly dependent on the tool set available in the study.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The case-study IPM rotors used spot-welded laminations around the outer edges.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: The welded lamination construction prevented individual permanent magnets from being removed by the non-destructive manual or robotic approaches assessed.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Lamination-stack joining method
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The result is specific to the assessed IPM constructions and the non-destructive methods available in the study.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: PM rotor removal involves strong destabilising magnetic forces acting across a small rotor-stator clearance.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Offset or contact between rotor and stator can increase friction, scoring, jamming and surface-damage risk.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Rotor-stator clearance; PM rotor present; available axial withdrawal path
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The experiment used a simplified 3D-printed rotor and precision-machined steel hub rather than an aged production motor.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Ability to maintain concentric axial withdrawal
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The centred, non-contact condition produced lower disassembly force than offset or contact conditions.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Maximum disassembly force was 38% lower than contact and 49% lower than the offset condition, showing that geometric alignment strongly affects separability and damage risk.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Straight axial access; alignment tolerance; obstruction to concentric withdrawal
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The relationship is experimentally supported, but the exact percentages are not universal design thresholds.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Axial fixation method of rotor stack / balancing disc
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The type of fixation determines whether preparation is needed before the lamination stack and balancing disc can be removed.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Some fixation types can only be released by damaging disassembly, whereas a press-fit configuration may avoid an additional preparation step.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Axial fixation method; reversible vs damaging connection
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The process chain was derived from a representative PMSM rotor and experimentally investigated on one small traction-motor rotor.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Shaft shoulders and interference / press fit
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Removal direction must account for shaft shoulders, while high concentricity and torque requirements can produce high press forces.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Shaft geometry and interference can constrain the direction and effort required to separate the rotor stack from the shaft.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Shaft shoulders; fit type; permitted removal direction
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The paper does not provide a universal force threshold for shaft-stack separation.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Lamination-stack segmentation and axial stack length
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Depending on rotor design, stack segments may be joined through the magnet fixation and may need to be separated before magnet removal.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Attempting to disassemble magnets through the full axial rotor-stack length can require large press forces and may destroy the magnets.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Stack segmentation; segment joining; axial stack length
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The finding identifies a design relationship but does not establish a universal maximum stack length.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Magnet fixation and magnets per pocket
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Buried magnets may be fixed by adhesive, transfer moulding or mechanical retention; the experiment showed different force behaviour depending on configuration.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Fixation type and the number of magnets in a slot influence extraction behaviour and required force.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Magnet fixation method; magnets per pocket; bonded contact
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The experimental series was small and used one rotor geometry and adhesive system; the paper warns against overgeneralising.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: NdFeB magnets are brittle and their protective coating must remain intact to prevent oxidation.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: High contact pressure or poorly matched tooling can damage the magnet or coating, reducing direct-reuse potential.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Magnet coating; magnet dimensions; expected contact stress
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The cited NdFeB compressive-strength range is broad, so it should not be used as a simple pass/fail threshold.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The disassembly cell had to accommodate wide ranges of magnet dimensions, lamination-stack dimensions and 12-40 magnet pockets.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Variation in magnet size, pocket count and rotor geometry is sufficiently large that these attributes need to be represented explicitly rather than treated as one standard rotor.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Magnet dimensions; pocket count; lamination-stack dimensions
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The dimensional ranges are requirements for the developed cell, not recommended design limits.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Magnet radial position within the rotor
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The developed cell could not reach magnet positions very close to the rotor centre without hardware adaptation.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Magnet radial position can affect physical accessibility, even when the magnet itself is otherwise removable.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Magnet radial position; distance from rotor centre
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The reported 26 mm limitation is specific to the developed cell and must not be used as a universal threshold.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Adhesive / fixation type and magnets per pocket
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Force-displacement behaviour differed from the earlier Heim study because a different adhesive was present and one rather than two magnets occupied each pocket.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: The result reinforces that fixation system and pocket configuration influence the physical difficulty of magnet removal.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Fixation type; adhesive; magnets per pocket
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The reported forces of roughly 10-14 kN are specific to the tested lamination stack and should not become generic thresholds.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Surface magnets are bonded on the rotor circumference, while buried magnets are enclosed within laminated rotor pockets.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Buried magnets have additional surrounding restraint and larger bonded interfaces, increasing the difficulty of intact separation.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Magnet topology; embedment; bonded surface area
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The component tests used laboratory specimens designed to mimic rotor-magnet connections.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Adhesive fixation is increasingly used to meet tolerances and protect magnets against vibration and coating damage.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: The same adhesive joint becomes an end-of-life barrier because the bond must be overcome without fracturing the magnet or contaminating the recovered surface.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Fixation method; adhesive present; adhesive type
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The study examined selected industrial adhesives rather than all possible fixation systems.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Purely mechanical shearing of 20 mm laboratory stacks fractured surface magnets; buried magnets could not be pushed out and the punches deformed.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Greater embedment and surrounding restraint can make intact removal infeasible under a simple mechanical separation condition.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Magnet topology; embedment depth; bonded area
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The exact 20 mm result belongs to the laboratory test geometry and must not be generalised as a universal limit.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Residual shear strength varied strongly between adhesive systems, particularly around and above their glass-transition temperatures.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Adhesive specification is relevant to how reversible a bonded magnet joint may be; 'adhesive bonded' alone is not sufficiently descriptive.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Adhesive type; glass-transition temperature; debonding capability
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: This identifies a material-design dependency. It does not imply that the evaluator must prescribe a particular heating process.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Adhesive residue, magnet fracture and surface condition
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Different separation conditions produced fracture, adhesive residue or surface discolouration on recovered magnets.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Successful physical removal and suitability for direct reuse are separate outcomes; recovered surface condition needs its own evaluation.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Expected residue; coating condition; visible damage
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: Surface-condition effects depend on the adhesive and treatment conditions used in the study.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Connection count, modularity and tool variety
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The review identifies simplified product design, low levels of assembly, modularity, minimal fastener use and fewer required tools as factors that facilitate disassembly.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: These attributes provide a general design-level description of whether a motor is easy or difficult to access and separate.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Connection count; modularity; fastener count; tool variety
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: These are synthesis findings drawn from wider disassembly literature rather than original EV-motor experiments in this paper.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The review distinguishes surface-mounted magnets from IPM magnets embedded within stacks of electrical-steel laminations.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Embedding changes the access route because the magnet is enclosed by the rotor structure rather than exposed on its surface.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Magnet topology: surface-mounted / buried
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The paper is a review and does not provide a universal numerical penalty for IPM topology.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The review notes that rotor-specific magnet-ejection concepts are constrained by magnet shape, dimensions and arrangement, which continue to evolve between rotor designs.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Geometry and arrangement influence whether evidence from one rotor is applicable to another.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Magnet dimensions; shape; arrangement; pocket geometry
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: This is a synthesis of earlier work rather than a controlled comparison performed by Li et al.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The review identifies product variability and manufacturing techniques as two major barriers to workable motor disassembly.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Motor design determines the assembly strategy and therefore the access and separation problems that appear at end of life.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Motor variant; assembly strategy; manufacturing / joining method
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluation output affected: Applicability of evidence; general disassembly burden
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The paper does not quantify the individual effect of each source of variability.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Small rotor-stator clearance in a PM motor
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The review notes that PM rotor removal while keeping the rotor concentric can require complex tooling because of significant magnetic forces and clearances of about 1 mm or less in many machines.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Small clearances make rotor-stator separation sensitive to misalignment and contact damage.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Rotor-stator clearance; accessibility for concentric removal
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: This is general electric-motor review evidence and does not provide an EV-specific force threshold.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The review states that magnets may be reusable after demagnetisation if they are not damaged during dismantling.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: The evaluator needs to distinguish 'removable' from 'recoverable in a condition suitable for reuse'.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Magnet damage state; coating / surface condition
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The paper does not define a quantitative reuse-condition threshold.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The paper describes disassembly as necessary to reach bearings, shaft, rotor, stator and windings for inspection, repair or remanufacture.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: This supports treating general motor disassemblability as relevant beyond magnet recovery alone.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Target component; preceding disassembly steps
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The illustrated Figure 1 is based on a 3-kW brake motor rather than an automotive traction motor.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The review argues that new electric machines should be designed with future reuse, refurbishment, remanufacture and recycling in mind.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Recoverability can legitimately be treated as a design-evaluation objective rather than only an end-of-life process problem.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Whether end-of-life access / recovery is represented in design information
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: This is a high-level circular-design conclusion, not technical evidence for a specific disassembly variable.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The review warns that changes to motor materials and design must also be assessed against efficiency and use-phase impacts.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: A recoverability evaluation should be presented as one design dimension, not as a complete sustainability assessment of the motor.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Motor efficiency / performance retained as external context
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The current workbook deliberately does not evaluate whole-life efficiency or environmental performance.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Conventional IPM rotors embed magnets deep inside rigid laminated cores, often in I-, V- or U-shaped cavities supported by iron ribs.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Deep embedment and iron ribs physically enclose the magnets and can make access dependent on destructive cutting or shredding, with risk of mixing magnet and steel material.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Magnet topology; cavity type; iron ribs present; degree of enclosure
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The conventional design is used as a comparator to a new prototype. The paper does not quantify a universal penalty for ribs or cavity depth.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The proposed rib-less IPM rotor eliminates adhesives and resins and retains magnets through cavity clamping, axial bolts and end plates.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Replacing permanent adhesive retention with reversible mechanical retention enabled non-destructive access to the magnet-containing rotor modules.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Adhesive or resin present; retention principle; reversible mechanical fastening
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluation output affected: Joint reversibility; intact magnet recovery feasibility
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: This is one prototype concept; it demonstrates feasibility rather than establishing a universal best fixation.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The proposed rotor separates the outer core into modules around an integral inner core, with positioning elements and end plates for alignment.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: A modular/segmented structure allows the rotor to be separated into discrete parts instead of treating the laminated rotor as one rigid inseparable body.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Rotor modularity; number of separable modules; positioning features
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: Modularity can introduce additional components and mechanical design requirements, so it should not automatically be treated as beneficial without context.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The rotor uses axial bolts and end plates as the primary mechanical retention system.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: The prototype was assembled and subsequently disassembled successfully without adhesives, supporting accessible reversible fasteners as a design feature linked to easier end-of-life separation.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Fastener reversibility; fastener accessibility; end-cap retention
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The disassembly demonstration was qualitative and did not report comparative disassembly time or effort.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The paper notes that conventional stator windings are commonly resin-impregnated to improve thermal and mechanical performance.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Resin impregnation complicates separation of copper windings from the steel core, showing that general motor disassemblability is affected by permanent material bonding beyond the rotor.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Stator impregnation / potting present; separability of winding and core
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: This is background synthesis rather than an experiment conducted in the paper, and it concerns stator material separation rather than magnet recovery.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The review describes SPM magnets as surface-accessible while IPM magnets are enclosed in rotor laminations and may require the rotor to be separated into skewed sections before access.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Magnet topology affects the number of structural barriers between the rotor surface and the magnet.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Magnet topology; rotor segmentation / skew; enclosure
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluation output affected: Magnet accessibility; number of preceding rotor-separation steps
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The paper synthesises earlier projects and does not provide a controlled original SPM-versus-IPM experiment.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The review reports that adhesives and resin casting used to secure magnets can be extremely difficult to remove and can leave contamination on recovered magnets.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Permanent material-locking around magnets reduces joint reversibility and can reduce recovered surface quality.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Adhesive present; resin / potting present; material-locking fixation
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluation output affected: Joint reversibility; intact removal feasibility; recovered condition
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: This is synthesis of prior disassembly trials, not a new experiment by Li et al.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The review identifies changing magnet shape between machine generations as a barrier to direct reuse and proposes smaller standardised segments as a way to improve compatibility.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: A recovered magnet can be intact yet still be difficult to reuse if its geometry is too product-specific.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Magnet shape standardisation; segment size; geometry compatibility
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The standardised-segment concept is illustrated mainly using non-EV examples and can introduce extra assembly complexity and adhesive use.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Modular design and mechanical support complexity
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The review notes that modular designs can improve general disassembly, but modules still require joints, brackets or other support structures.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Modularity should therefore be evaluated together with the number and reversibility of the connections needed to hold the modules.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Modularity; module-support connections; bracket / joint complexity
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: This is a qualitative design synthesis rather than a quantified motor comparison.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The review reports that coating type affects whether NdFeB magnets retain acceptable surface and corrosion protection after repeated thermal cycles.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Coating specification can influence whether an intact recovered magnet remains suitable for direct reuse.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Magnet coating type; coating condition
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The coating results are taken from an earlier study and the thermal-cycle context should not be generalised to all recovery routes.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The paper reports earlier MORE-project findings that magnets from SPM machines were easier to disassemble than magnets from IPM machines when considering access and post-disassembly magnet quality among the comparison factors.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Surface placement can improve magnet accessibility relative to buried placement.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Magnet topology: surface-mounted / buried
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The comparison is reported from an earlier project rather than reproduced experimentally in this paper, and SPM traction designs have different performance constraints.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: High-speed SPM designs require a retention sleeve over surface magnets, commonly carbon fibre or polyester.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Even when magnets are surface-mounted, an external retention layer can form an additional access barrier and should be recorded separately from topology.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Retention sleeve / bandage present; sleeve material
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The paper analyses the sleeve primarily as a performance constraint and does not experimentally quantify its disassembly burden.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The paper shows that a magnet-reuse-oriented SPM design can reduce active magnetic length because of glue space, while traction requirements may favour other motor configurations.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: A design feature that improves reuse or disassembly can also alter motor performance, so recoverability should remain one evaluation dimension rather than the sole design objective.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Recoverability-related design change present
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: This is a performance study of mild-hybrid SPM designs and should not be used to score current recoverability.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Across the studied EV components, magnets could not be extracted intact in most cases.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Current production designs frequently contain structural or joining barriers that prevent straightforward intact magnet recovery.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Intact magnet physically accessible?; destructive access required?
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The study covers selected Fiat and Jeep vehicle components in Italy and does not provide controlled comparison of individual design variables.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Many studied components were joined using welding or resins, and an angle grinder was often required to reach the magnets.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Irreversible joining methods increase destructive access requirements and reduce practical disassemblability.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Joining method: welded / resin-bonded / reversible
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluation output affected: General disassembly burden; destructive access requirement
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The paper reports practical dismantling observations but does not isolate the individual time penalty of welding versus resin.
evidenceRegister.Source location: Disassembly of magnets from the rotor; page 10

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: In several studied motors and components, magnets were sealed inside the rotor by a steel plate.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: A permanent cover or sealing plate creates an additional physical barrier between the rotor exterior and the magnets.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Rotor cover / steel plate present; cover removability
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The study highlights the barrier partly in relation to hydrogen access, but the underlying design issue is physical enclosure of the magnets.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The authors conclude that ecodesign and standardisation of motor assembly and disassembly are important to make magnet dismantling and recovery practically viable.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Low standardisation and product-specific permanent joints contribute to high recovery effort.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Assembly standardisation; connection standardisation
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: This is a conclusion from the case-study observations rather than a quantified standardisation metric.
evidenceRegister.Source location: Disassembly of magnets from the rotor; page 10

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The paper identifies caulking, press fits with sacrificial layers, injection moulding, structural adhesives and spring-based fixation as distinct rotor magnet-retention approaches.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Fixation category is a primary design attribute because different joining principles create different levels of permanence and separability.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Magnet fixation method; force/form/material locking
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The comparison of conventional fixation approaches is literature-based background within a concept paper.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The paper distinguishes conventional robust but generally permanent fixation from a proposed interlayer intended to provide operational retention and controlled release.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: The evaluator should record not only how a magnet is fixed, but whether the fixation was intentionally designed to be reversible.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Designed release mechanism present?; reversible fixation trigger
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The proposed hygroscopic fixation has only analytical and simulation support and still requires experimental validation.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: A reversible fixation concept must still withstand rotor temperature, centrifugal loading, vibration and environmental exposure during service.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: A design should not be considered recoverable solely because it has a release mechanism; operational robustness and release conditions must also be known.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Fixation operating-temperature range; environmental sensitivity; release condition
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The specific sub-100 °C condition belongs to the proposed hygroscopic concept and is not a general recoverability threshold.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The direct-reuse concept uses several small standard-sized magnets rather than one product-specific solid magnet pole.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Standardised segmentation can make intact recovered magnets more compatible with future applications because the recovered unit is less tied to one pole geometry.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Magnet segmentation; standard dimensions; geometry standardisation
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The segmentation concept originates from the authors' wind-turbine study rather than an EV traction-motor experiment, so transfer to high-speed EV rotors requires caution.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Zn, epoxy, Ni-Cu-Ni and Ni-Cu+epoxy coatings were compared after zero, one and five Curie-temperature heat cycles.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: The coating system strongly affected post-treatment corrosion protection; Ni-Cu+epoxy showed the best overall stability while Zn and epoxy degraded more strongly.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Magnet coating type; protective layer system
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluation output affected: Recovered surface condition; corrosion resistance; direct-reuse potential
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The test isolates magnets rather than magnets inside an EV rotor, and the result is specific to the tested coatings and thermal-demagnetisation conditions.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Most magnets retained comparable magnetic properties after one and five Curie-temperature cycles even though coating corrosion performance differed substantially.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Recovered-magnet condition should not be represented by a single outcome because magnetic performance and protective-coating integrity can diverge.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Magnetic performance; coating integrity
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: One epoxy batch was accidentally heated to about 650 °C and is explicitly treated by the authors as invalid for the intended comparison.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The review identifies adhesives and epoxy resins as conventional magnet-integration mechanisms that hinder efficient recovery, while mechanical fasteners or snap-fit type connections can enable non-destructive isolation.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: How the magnet is integrated into the motor is a design-level determinant of whether it can be separated without destroying the magnet or surrounding structure.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Magnet fixation / integration method; reversible connection present
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluation output affected: Joint reversibility; intact magnet isolation feasibility
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: This is a literature-based overview and does not experimentally compare the proposed alternative fixation methods.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The review identifies magnet composition, weight, coating and location as information that supports reuse, remanufacturing and end-of-life handling, potentially through a digital product passport.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: The evaluator needs explicit magnet metadata as well as geometry; otherwise the applicability of recovery and reuse evidence is difficult to determine.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Magnet composition; mass; coating; location; identifier / traceability
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluation output affected: Data completeness; evaluation confidence; reuse/remanufacture assessment
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The paper proposes information requirements at value-chain level; it does not validate a specific digital product-passport schema for EV motors.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The paper distinguishes magnets as intact, failed or broken, with different circular pathways associated with those conditions.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Physical recovery is not the final evaluation outcome; the recovered magnet's condition determines whether higher-value reuse remains possible.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Recovered integrity; magnetic condition
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluation output affected: Reuse potential; remanufacture potential; material-recycling route
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The intact/failed/broken classification is conceptual and not accompanied by quantitative condition thresholds.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: In the original claw-pole design, a magnet slit terminates at the end of the inter-claw and obstructs magnet removal; the reuse-oriented concept extends the slit through the second claw-pole.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: A continuous extraction path can determine whether an otherwise accessible magnet can physically leave the rotor without destructive opening of the surrounding structure.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Magnet pocket/slit open or closed; continuous exit path; extraction direction
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluation output affected: Intact magnet removal feasibility; magnet accessibility
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The case is a 48 V mild-hybrid claw-pole machine rather than a conventional IPM traction rotor, and the paper presents the reuse-oriented geometry as a design methodology rather than a broad comparative experiment.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Varnish is applied over the claw-poles, rotor winding, magnets and shaft for vibration, corrosion and thermal reasons.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: A coating or varnish that bridges several rotor components acts as an additional material lock and must be removed or weakened before magnet separation.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Varnish / encapsulation present; components covered; material-locking layer
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The paper does not quantify the disassembly penalty of the varnish itself and discusses several possible removal methods that are outside the present evaluation scope.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Standardisation of parts, materials, tools and processes
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The WIRE framework treats standard materials, standard tools and conventional assembly/disassembly processes as distinct contributors to motor recyclability.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: This supports recording standardisation and special-process dependence as design/evaluation attributes, even though the paper's numerical scores are not adopted here.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Material standardisation; tool standardisation; special process required
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: WIRE scores are relative, partly expert-derived and scenario-dependent. The present evidence base uses the identified factors only, not the published scoring scale.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Motor volume and air-gap flux density
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The authors propose that rotor-stator separation becomes more difficult as motor volume and air-gap flux density increase because magnetic extraction forces become larger.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Motor scale and magnetic loading may be relevant contextual variables when estimating the difficulty of separating a PM rotor from its stator.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Motor active volume; air-gap flux density
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The relationship is an analytical scoring assumption within WIRE, not a universally validated physical threshold or predictive equation.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Across four DEMETER motor concepts, the WIRE comparison assigned better disassembly outcomes to simpler structures without glue and poorer outcomes where magnets were glued or required special processing for extraction.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: The comparison reinforces adhesive use and structural complexity as separate design features that can obstruct magnet recovery.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Adhesive / glue present; rotor structural complexity; special access step required
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluation output affected: Magnet recovery difficulty; general disassembly burden
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The comparison is produced through the WIRE scoring framework, so the numerical differences reflect expert assumptions and should not be treated as empirical effect sizes.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: WIRE is explicitly described as a relative comparison method whose scores depend on common scaling assumptions and agreement among an expert group.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: The published WIRE scores should not be imported directly as objective training labels; the underlying variables and evidence are more transferable than the numerical scores.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Evaluation method provenance; expert judgement dependence
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: This row records a limitation of the evaluation approach rather than a motor-design characteristic.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Zn, Ni/Cu/Ni and epoxy coatings responded differently to thermal demagnetisation at 380 °C.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Coating choice can determine whether an extracted magnet retains corrosion protection and magnetic performance suitable for direct reuse; Ni/Cu/Ni was the most stable of the tested systems.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Magnet coating type; coating material system
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluation output affected: Recovered condition; corrosion protection; reuse potential
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The study evaluates isolated magnets under one thermal-demagnetisation regime. It does not establish a universal best coating for every motor or recovery route.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The three commercial Nd-Fe-B grades had different compositions and measured Curie temperatures of about 290, 310 and 340 °C.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Magnet grade or composition is relevant metadata because recovery conditions that are benign for one grade may affect another differently.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Magnet grade; chemical composition; Curie temperature
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: This relationship is particularly relevant when reuse assessment includes thermal demagnetisation; it should not become a generic recoverability score by itself.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Some samples recovered their magnetic performance after remagnetisation even when the protective coating had materially changed or degraded.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: An evaluation should keep magnetic performance, coating integrity and corrosion protection as separate recovered-condition outputs rather than collapsing them into a single 'recovered/not recovered' result.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Magnetic-property retention; coating integrity; corrosion protection
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The finding is based on the three tested coating systems and thermal conditions.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The authors note that even when a suitable demagnetisation and coating combination exists, magnet recovery may remain impossible because of the complex configuration of the magnet-containing device.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Material-level reuse suitability does not replace structural design evaluation; accessibility and fixation must be assessed independently.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Structural accessibility; material reuse suitability
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The statement is a general conclusion rather than a quantified comparison of motor architectures.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The review treats the motor as separable case, stator and rotor subassemblies and states that remanufacturing requires disassembly when one or more critical components must be reprocessed or replaced.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: General motor disassemblability should consider whether major functional subassemblies can be accessed and separated rather than treating the motor only as one indivisible product.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Subsystem boundaries; separability of case, stator and rotor
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: This is a broad automotive e-motor review. Where automotive evidence was unavailable, the authors explicitly considered evidence from other electric-motor sectors.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The review notes that IPM magnets are pressed from rotor segments using rotor-specific ejectors, while SPM recovery first requires the external retention bandage issue to be resolved.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Surface placement does not guarantee immediate access, while buried placement introduces rotor-core enclosure and geometry-specific access constraints.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Magnet topology; rotor segmentation; retention bandage present
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The paper synthesises prior studies and demonstrators rather than performing a controlled SPM-versus-IPM extraction experiment.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Availability of product design and usage information
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The review states that reuse and remanufacturing require strong knowledge of the motor and cites electronic data logs and digital product passports as ways to preserve design and usage information.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Evaluation confidence improves when the motor's design identity, previous use and component information are available rather than inferred after end of life.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Product identifier; design information; usage history
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: This concerns information availability rather than a physical disassembly characteristic, and the paper does not validate one standard data schema.
evidenceRegister.Source location: Reuse and remanufacturing discussion; journal pp. 328-329

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The Tesla Model Y EDU was secured by approximately 40 bolts distributed across three main joining interfaces.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: A high number of fasteners distributed across multiple interfaces contributes directly to the amount of separation work required before the motor subassemblies are accessible.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Fastener count; number of joining interfaces
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The numerical count is specific to the investigated Tesla Model Y EDU and should not become a universal threshold.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Selective access to the rotor core required disconnection of phase terminals and resolver, separation of the electric-motor module from the main EDU, and only then extraction of the rotor from the encased stator.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: The architecture creates a dependency chain in which upstream components and interfaces must be cleared before the rotor can be reached.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Preceding components; component hierarchy; access sequence
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The sequence is specific to the Model Y architecture, although the study also reports disassembly of four additional EoL motor units with different configurations.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Some modules resisted separation after mechanical fasteners had been removed; this was notably observed at interfaces using metal gaskets where separation force was still required.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: An interface can remain mechanically resistant after fastener removal, so gasket or seal design can affect separability independently of fastener count.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Gasket / seal present; interface sealing method
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: Only two of the five evaluated motor modules contained gaskets at their interface joints, and the paper does not provide a universal force value.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The EDU contained bespoke fasteners with thread sizes from M4 to M10, and corroded fastener heads sometimes impeded tool engagement.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Fastener variety increases tool-selection complexity, while condition can further reduce practical accessibility at end of life.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Fastener type; thread-size range; bespoke fastener present
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: Corrosion is an end-of-life condition rather than a design characteristic; the evaluator should keep fastener design and product condition separate.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The electric-motor module weighed about 42 kg and contained sensitive features such as the shaft spindle and phase terminals, requiring careful coordinated handling during separation.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Large, heavy and tightly integrated modules increase handling constraints and the risk of collateral damage during component separation.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Subassembly mass; handling access; sensitive adjacent features
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The 42 kg value is specific to the Model Y motor module and should not be used as a universal limit.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Small air gap, bearing support and magnetic retention
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Rotor-core removal from the encased stator had to overcome mechanical resistance from the front bearing and magnetic retention from the embedded permanent magnets; scuffing and collisions were observed during retrieval.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Rotor-stator separability depends on the combined geometry and support arrangement, not only magnetic attraction, and poor separation can damage otherwise reusable components.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Rotor-stator clearance; bearing support arrangement; axial access path
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The paper does not report a measured air-gap dimension or a general force model for this production motor.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The reference traction-drive study identifies pins, screws, adhesives, sealants and press fits as possible joining features between the bearing shield and housing.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: The type and combination of joints at a major access interface determine how easily the housing can be opened without destructive separation.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: End-shield joining method; screws/pins; adhesive; sealant; press fit
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The paper combines a reference series drive with literature research, dismantling trials and expert assessment; individual joining methods are not isolated experimentally.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The paper distinguishes force-fit, form-fit and material-fit stator-housing connections. Thermally created friction fits can be reversed with relatively few limitations, whereas gluing adds additional separation difficulty.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Stator-housing joining principle is a distinct design variable because some connections are inherently more reversible than material-bonded alternatives.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Stator-housing joining method; shrink fit; adhesive present
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The discussion is based on a representative drive plus literature and expert-supported dismantling evaluation rather than a controlled comparison of identical motors.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The paper states that stator epoxy encapsulation currently requires destructive removal and that thermoplastic overmoulding further complicates recycling.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Material encapsulation can prevent clean separation of windings and laminated cores even after the stator has been removed from the housing.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Stator encapsulation present; resin / overmoulding type
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The statement concerns current available processing routes and does not quantify the penalty for different resin formulations.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Distributed windings and hairpins can be removed axially, while continuous distributed windings with closed-form coils require radial disassembly.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Winding architecture determines the feasible extraction direction and therefore changes the physical disassembly path through the stator.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Winding type; coil closure; axial or radial extraction path
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The paper describes common design-dependent routes rather than reporting comparative extraction times for each winding type.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The rotor core and shaft may use frictional, positive or material connections, including shrink fits, press-out connections and machine elements.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: The joining principle between rotor core and shaft determines whether the rotor can be separated reversibly and what direction or force must be applied.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Rotor-core/shaft joining method; shrink fit; machine elements
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The paper does not provide one universal preferred joint or force threshold.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Depending on the cooling concept, the stator may be embedded in a separate cooling jacket; separate jackets are often fixed with screw connections.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Cooling-system integration changes the number and type of interfaces that must be separated before the stator and housing are fully dismantled.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Cooling jacket present; integrated or separate; joining method
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The paper describes representative industrial configurations rather than comparing identical motors with different cooling-jacket designs.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: In the exemplary traction-drive dismantling sequence, the housing was secured by six distinct screw types, with some screws obscured by dirt or debris.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: A high variety of connection types and poor visibility of connection points make access and tool selection more difficult before deeper components can be reached.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Fastener type count; connection-point visibility; occlusion
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The paper presents an exemplary dismantling trial rather than a statistically representative sample of all EV traction drives.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Hidden fasteners and preceding gearbox removal
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Additional screws securing the electric-motor housing cover were located beneath the gearbox, so the gearbox cover and gearbox had to be removed before the rotor could be accessed.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Fastener placement can create mandatory preceding operations even when the target rotor is physically close to the housing surface.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Hidden fasteners; obstructing components; preceding removal count
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The sequence is specific to the investigated traction-drive architecture.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The paper states that different motor types require different disassembly process chains and that high design variance makes standardised dismantling difficult.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Evidence and disassembly assumptions must be matched to the actual motor architecture rather than transferred blindly between traction-drive designs.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Motor type; integration degree; architecture variant
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: This is a general conclusion supported by project experience rather than a quantified relationship between variance and disassembly time.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Multiple joining principles within one motor assembly
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The described PMSM assembly chain uses screwed or glued housing parts, pressed shafts and bearings, a thermally shrunk stator-housing interface and sealing operations.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: A single traction motor can contain several different joint classes, so general disassemblability depends on the combined reversibility of multiple interfaces rather than one connector type alone.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Joining-method diversity; number of joint classes; sealing present
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The assembly chain is presented as a standard process description and not as a measured teardown comparison.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Number and type of preceding disassembly steps
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: For Volkswagen electric motors, the authors developed a 14-step manual disassembly guide before the rotor was exposed. The preceding operations included levering off covers, removing retaining rings and pulling out shafts.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Rotor access can depend on a substantial chain of mechanical removals before any magnet-level recovery is possible.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Number of preceding steps; access-layer count; preceding component types
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The 14-step count is specific to the analysed Volkswagen motor architecture and the authors' selected disassembly boundary.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Screw accessibility, tool changes and gripping points
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Manual dismantling workshops recorded tool changes, screw accessibility and gripping points needed to loosen components, and these observations were used to revise the dismantling sequence.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Connection accessibility and available gripping features are design-level contributors to whether components can be reached and separated efficiently.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Tool access clearance; gripping point availability; tool-change requirement
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluation output affected: General disassembly burden; component access difficulty
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The paper does not provide universal clearance or gripping-dimension thresholds.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Difference between nominal CAD data and actual returned motor
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The authors compared CAD information with the actual motor and documented differences, ageing, wear and variations in connection technologies before disassembly.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: A model based only on nominal design data may not fully represent the as-returned product; provenance and actual-state information affect confidence in a disassembly evaluation.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: CAD/as-built consistency; product condition; connection-state information
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: Ageing and wear are end-of-life condition variables rather than design characteristics and should remain separate from design evaluation where possible.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Rotor stack retained by removable axial screws
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: In the Volkswagen rotor, four long M6 x 125 mm screws secure the rotor stack. After loosening them, the balance discs and laminated cores containing the magnets can be pressed off the shaft; the authors report that the magnets were then driven from the laminations with minimal manual effort.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: A rotor architecture using accessible removable axial fasteners can create a clear separation route from the assembled rotor to magnet-containing lamination sections.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Rotor-stack retention method; through-bolt count; removable balance discs; stack-to-shaft separability
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: This is one Volkswagen rotor design. The reported ease of final magnet removal must not be generalised to other IPM rotors or fixation systems.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Manual disassembly of two used traction motors, a Volkswagen ID.3 motor and an e.go motor, found that although the motors were constructed differently, the main joining processes were broadly similar and fell into putting-together, press-on/press-in and bonding groups.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Connection type is a transferable design descriptor that can structure disassembly evidence across different traction-motor architectures.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Joining-process family; connection type
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: Only two motors were examined, so the three groups should be treated as a useful classification rather than proof that all traction motors use the same joint set.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Retaining rings were used in all analysed motors to secure the rotor-shaft bearing axially. Their removal was rated medium to difficult because the operation is kinematically complex and access can be very limited.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Small axial-retention components can become important disassembly barriers when their access and deformation path are constrained.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Retaining ring present; retaining-ring accessibility; removal clearance
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluation output affected: Bearing/shaft access difficulty; general disassembly burden
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The difficulty rating is qualitative and based on the two manually disassembled motors.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Screw joints were common in housings and sensors and were normally non-destructively detachable, but corrosion or wear in used products could make destructive removal necessary.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: The same nominal reversible fastener can have different practical separability at end of life, so fastener design and returned-product condition should be represented separately.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Screw connection present; fastener condition; corrosion/wear state
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: Corrosion and wear are condition variables rather than inherent design attributes.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The analysed motors used press joints for bearings with interference fits; the authors report that these could be loosened non-destructively using a suitable pulling tool and rated them easy to disassemble.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: A press or interference fit should not automatically be treated as a severe barrier; its effect depends on geometry, access and whether a defined pulling route is available.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Interference fit present; pull-off access; bearing fit arrangement
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: This finding concerns the examined bearing fits and does not establish that all interference fits are easy to reverse.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Housing sealant acting as a bonded joint
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Sealant used on housing parts produced adhesive bonding that prevented easy component removal. The sealant itself had to be destroyed and its poor accessibility led to a medium-to-difficult qualitative rating.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Sealing material can function as an unintended adhesive joint, creating separation resistance even when bonding is not its primary design purpose.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Sealant/adhesive present; bonded interface area; adhesive accessibility
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The rating is qualitative and based on the sealants encountered in two motors.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The proposed motor model represents the motor as Parts and Connections. Each connection stores the joint type and movement constraints; non-geometric metadata are explicitly required for threaded, glue and retaining-ring connections in addition to geometry-derived contacts.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: A CAD-based evaluator needs more than component geometry. It also needs connection semantics and the directions in which each connection constrains separation.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Part identity; connected-part pair; connection type; movement constraints; screw-head type
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The model is a planning representation rather than a validated quantitative recoverability score.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Target-specific partial disassembly and incomplete cost metrics
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The graph can be searched until a specific target part or subset is removed rather than requiring complete motor disassembly. The implemented cost metric is only part-to-part centre-of-mass distance; tool changes, process time and destructiveness are identified as future metrics.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: The eventual evaluator can be target-specific, such as reaching the rotor or magnets, but this paper's current optimisation metric should not be imported as a disassemblability score.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Target component / target disassembly state; metric provenance
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The planning framework had not yet implemented process time, tool changes or destructiveness as costs.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Hierarchical parent-child dependency in motor disassembly
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The CE model represents the motor as a hierarchical disassembly tree in which lower-level parts, including permanent magnets, can only be recovered to the extent that their parent subassemblies are disassembled.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: Evaluation of magnet recoverability should preserve the assembly hierarchy because access to a lower-level target depends on successful separation of upper-level motor subassemblies.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Parent subassembly; child component; hierarchy level; preceding-disassembly dependency
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The numerical outcome percentages in the paper's example are hypothetical assumptions rather than measured disassembly data.

evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Table 1 assigns percentages to inventory, further disassembly, recycling and landfill for each motor subassembly, but the authors explicitly describe the table as a hypothetical example based on assumptions.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: These percentages are useful for demonstrating model logic but must not be used as empirical training labels or evidence-based recoverability probabilities.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Model assumption provenance
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: Empirical condition and outcome data are identified as something that may become available in future through non-destructive evaluation.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Disassembly-process data omitted from life-cycle and cost model
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: The study excludes EV collection, non-destructive evaluation, disassembly operations and landfill treatment from parts of the LCA because of missing data, and does not include disassembly labour costs because a detailed process plan was unavailable.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: The paper cannot provide empirical disassembly time, labour or process-impact labels for our evaluator even though it provides a useful structural modelling approach.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Missing-data flag; evidence type
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The authors state that adding these processes in future could affect the results.

evidenceRegister.Design feature: Sensitivity to upper-level versus lower-level subassembly outcomes
evidenceRegister.Design condition / state: Within the authors' assumed CE model, changing outcomes for upper-level motor subassemblies had a larger effect on the evaluated CE objectives than changing lower-level parts.
evidenceRegister.Evidence-backed effect on disassemblabil: This supports the importance of representing high-level assembly access and reuse decisions in a system model rather than modelling only individual magnets.
evidenceRegister.Potential evaluator input: Assembly hierarchy level; upper-level outcome
evidenceRegister.Scope / limitation: The sensitivity result follows from the paper's assumed outcome structure and objectives; it is not direct physical evidence that upper-level joints are harder to disassemble.

Metric 1: Design Evaluation Cycle Time Reduction
Define the traditional design review cycle as the time required to take one concept from input to a completed circularity/DfD assessment.

Measure the time from:

design issue identified → revised design assessed.

Traditional baseline:

Selected concept → manual CAD/drawing review → manual DfD guideline assessment → expert discussion → identify issues → redesign → manual re-assessment

Digital system:

Selected concept → CAD/drawing import → automated DfD/circularity evaluation → issue identification → design recommendations → revised concept → re-evaluation

T (traditional) = average time to complete one design evaluation cycle using current methods.
